l: Sacred War, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Sacred War ended ten years after the Phocians seized the temple. Its conclusion was followed by changes to the Amphictyonic Council, including the admission of the Macedonians and the exclusion of the Phocians and Lacedæmonians.

l: Augustus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Augustus wished the inhabitants of Nicopolis near Actium to belong to the Amphictyonic Council. He joined the Magnetes, Malienses, Ænianes, and Phthiotes to the Thessalians and transferred their votes, along with those of the extinct Dolopes, to Nicopolis.

l: Nicopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Nicopolis near Actium was admitted to the Amphictyonic Council at the wish of Augustus. In the narrator’s time it supplied six members and sent delegates to every Amphictyonic Council.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Delphi was the meeting place of the Amphictyonic delegates and contained four temples in a row, including the temple of Athene Pronoia. Near Delphi were the sacred enclosure of Phylacus, the gymnasium, the river Plistus, and the spring of Castalia.

l: Amphictyonic Council, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Amphictyonic Council changed after the Sacred War, when the Macedonians were admitted and the Phocians and Lacedæmonians were excluded; the Phocians were later restored after their bravery against Brennus. Augustus transferred several votes to Nicopolis, and in the narrator’s time the Council had thirty members, with Athens, Delphi, and Nicopolis sending delegates to every meeting.

l: temple of Athene Pronoia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The temple of Athene Pronoia was the fourth of four temples encountered on entering Delphi. Its ante-chapel contained a large brass statue offered by the Massaliotes, while the golden shield offered by Crœsus had been removed, according to the Delphians, by Philomelus.

l: Massaliotes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Massaliotes offered a large brass statue in the ante-chapel of the temple of Athene Pronoia. They were colonists of the Phocæans in Ionia, descended from those who fled Phocæa from Harpagus the Mede, and they later prospered after defeating the Carthaginians in a naval engagement.

l: Phocæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Phocæans in Ionia founded the Massaliotes’ colony. Some of them had fled Phocæa from Harpagus the Mede before the Massaliotes defeated the Carthaginians and obtained the land they occupied.

l: Castalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Castalia was a drinkable spring on the road from the gymnasium to the temple at Delphi. Its name was variously attributed to a local woman or to a man called Castalius, while Panyasis said that Castalia was the daughter of Achelous; the people of Lilæa believed its water came from the Cephisus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Delphi is described as a very hilly town whose large sacred precincts of Apollo contain numerous votive offerings. These include statues and dedications from the Corcyraeans, Tegeans, Lacedæmonians, and others, commemorating victories, legends, and military actions. The text recounts the Corcyraeans’ offering after sacrificing a bull to Poseidon and catching a great shoal of tunny fish. It also describes monuments connected with the battle of Ægos-potamoi and with the conflict between the Lacedæmonians and Argives beyond Thyrea.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Delphi is everywhere hilly, and its sacred precincts and other parts of the town share this character. The town contains many votive offerings, including monuments connected with athletic victories, military events, local heroes, and legendary traditions.

l: sacred precincts of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The sacred precincts of Apollo are very large, lie in the upper part of Delphi, and have several entrances. They contain numerous votive offerings, including statues dedicated by the Corcyræans, Tegeans, and Lacedæmonians.

l: votive offerings, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The votive offerings at Delphi include Phayllus of Croton, a bronze bull dedicated by the Corcyræans, statues commemorating Tegean spoils from the Lacedæmonians, and statues dedicated by the Lacedæmonians after defeating the Athenians. Other offerings commemorate the Spartans and their allies at Ægos-potamoi, as well as the Argives’ claimed victory beyond Thyrea.

l: Aegospotami battle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Lacedæmonians dedicated statues at Delphi to commemorate their victory over the Athenians at Ægos-potamoi, including figures of Lysander, his prophet Abas, his pilot Hermon, and Spartan or allied participants. The Athenians claimed that their defeat resulted from the bribery of their admirals Tydeus and Adimantus by Lysander, citing Sibylline and Musæan oracles in support of this accusation.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The unit describes statues at Delphi dedicated from the tenth of the spoils of Marathon, including figures connected with Athens and its tribes. It also records Argive offerings commemorating victories at Oenoe and the expedition against Thebes, as well as offerings connected with restoring the Messenians. The Tarentines are represented by bronze horses and captive women, and the history of Tarentum’s colonization by Phalanthus is recounted. Phalanthus interpreted an oracle from Delphi through the name of his wife Æthra and captured Tarentum.

l: Battle of Marathon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The tenth of the spoils of Marathon was used for statues of Athene, Apollo, Miltiades, several heroes, and other figures associated with Athens. These statues were made by Phidias.

l: statues dedicated from the tenth of the spoils of Marathon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: These included Athene, Apollo, Miltiades, Erechtheus, Cecrops, Pandion, Leos, Antiochus, Ægeus, Acamas, Codrus, Theseus, and Phyleus. Antigonus, Demetrius, and Ptolemy were sent to Delphi later, with Ptolemy sent through goodwill and the Macedonians through fear.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: An oracle from Delphi determined names for the Athenian tribes. Statues of Antigonus, Demetrius, and Ptolemy were later sent to Delphi.

l: Argives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Argives dedicated statues of those associated with Polynices’ expedition against Thebes, along with the chariot of Amphiaraus and other figures. They said these offerings were made from spoils won at Oenoe in Argolis with Athenian allies, and they also erected statues of the Epigoni and figures connected with restoring the Messenians.

l: Messenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Messenians were restored with the assistance of the Argives, who supported Epaminondas and the Thebans.

l: Tarentum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Tarentum was described as the greatest and most prosperous of the maritime cities held by the barbarians in Italy. Phalanthus captured it after understanding an oracle from Delphi.

l: Phalanthus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Phalanthus led the Lacedæmonian colonization of Tarentum under an oracle from Delphi. After initially failing to capture a city or gain land, he interpreted the oracle through his wife Æthra’s tears and captured Tarentum on the following night.

l: oracle from Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The oracle told Phalanthus that he would acquire land and found a city where he saw rain from a clear sky. He eventually understood this as referring to his wife Æthra, whose name meant "clear sky," and then captured Tarentum.

l: foundation of Tarentum, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Tarentum was founded through the Lacedæmonian colonization led by Phalanthus. The city and its river were said to have received their names from the hero Taras, who was the son of Poseidon and a local Nymph.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The unit describes treasuries and votive offerings at Delphi, including those of the Sicyonians, Siphnii, Thebans, Athenians, Syracusans, and Potidaeans. The Cnidians dedicated statues near the Sicyonian treasury, while the people of Lipara dedicated statues after a naval victory over the Tyrrhenians. It recounts how the Siphnii built their treasury from the wealth of Siphnos's gold mines but lost the mines after ceasing their tribute to Delphi. It also describes Athenian offerings and a portico funded by war spoils from victories over Peloponnesians and other Greek allies.

l: treasury of the Sicyonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The treasury of the Sicyonians stands near the votive offering of the Tarentines, but it contains no money, like the other treasuries. Statues brought by the Cnidians stand beside it.

l: Sicyonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Sicyonians have a treasury at Delphi, although no money is present in it.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Delphi is the site of several treasuries, votive offerings, and dedications described in this unit. The Siphnii were instructed by the god to send a tenth of their gold-mining revenue there.

l: Cnidians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Cnidians brought statues to Delphi, including Triopas standing by a horse and Leto, Apollo, and Artemis shooting at the wounded Tityus. They were also the founders or colonists associated with Lipara, and their leader was said to have been Pentathlus.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Apollo received the Siphnii's required tenth at Delphi. The people of Cleonæ sent him a brazen goat after sacrificing a goat to the rising sun and being delivered from a plague.

l: Siphnian treasury, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Siphnian treasury was built after the god instructed the Siphnii to send a tenth of the revenue from Siphnos's gold mines to Delphi. The Siphnii sent this tenth until they ceased the tribute in their cupidity.

l: Siphnii, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Siphnii possessed gold mines on Siphnos and were instructed to send a tenth of their revenue to Delphi. After they stopped paying the tribute, the sea encroached and swept away their mines.

l: Siphnos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Siphnos had gold mines whose revenue supported the Siphnii's tribute to Delphi and the construction of the Siphnian treasury. The sea later encroached on the island and destroyed the mines after the tribute was discontinued.

l: Lipara, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The people of Lipara, a colony of Cnidians, erected statues after a naval victory over the Tyrrhenians. Lipara was one of the islands occupied by the colonists associated with the islands of Æolus.

l: Sicily, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Sicily is discussed through Antiochus the Syracusan's account of the Cnidian colonists. The colonists built a town at Pachynus but were expelled by the Elymi and Phœnicians before occupying islands including Lipara.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Athenians built treasuries from the victory at Marathon and the spoil taken from Datis. They also built a portico with money gained in war from the Peloponnesians and their Greek allies, and dedicated figure-heads of captured ships and brazen shields.

l: Marathon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The victory at Marathon and the spoil taken from Datis provided the basis for the Athenian treasuries at Delphi.

l: Athenian portico, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Athenian portico was built with money the Athenians obtained in war from the Peloponnesians and their Greek allies. Nearby were votive figure-heads of captured ships and brazen shields bearing an inscription naming the cities from which the spoil came.

l: Peloponnesians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Peloponnesians and other Greek allies were among those from whom the Athenians obtained war money used to build the Athenian portico.

l: naval victories of the Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Athenians commemorated their naval victories with figure-heads of captured ships, brazen shields, and sacrifices to Theseus and Poseidon at the promontory of Rhium. The inscription lists Elis, Lacedæmon, Sicyon, Megara, Pellene in Achaia, Ambracia, Leucas, and Corinth among the cities connected with the spoil.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The unit discusses the Herophiles, especially the first and second Herophile, their origins, prophecies, travels, and associations with Apollo. It describes the projecting stone at Delphi where the first Herophile was said to have chanted oracles, and records the second Herophile’s predictions concerning Helen and the fall of Ilium. It also recounts traditions about Herophile’s tomb in the Troad, competing claims about her birthplace, and other prophetically inspired women and men, including Demo, Sabbe, Phaennis, the Peleae, Euclus, Musaeus, Lycus, and Bacis.

l: Sibyl, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The first Herophile, also called the Sibyl, was regarded as extremely ancient and as the first woman to chant oracles. The Greeks said she was the daughter of Zeus and Lamia, the daughter of Poseidon, while the Libyans called her Sibyl.

l: second Herophile, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The second Herophile was younger than the first but lived before the Trojan War. She foretold that Helen would be raised in Sparta, causing the ruin of Asia Minor and Europe, and that Ilium would be captured by the Greeks; she was also associated with Samos, Clarus, Delos, and Delphi, and was said to have died in the Troad.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Apollo is associated with the Herophiles and their oracles. The second Herophile called herself Apollo’s wedded wife and sister and daughter when possessed by the god, and her tomb was located in the grove of Sminthian Apollo.

l: Delphians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Delphians said that the first Herophile chanted her oracles on a projecting stone above Delphi.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Greeks said that the first Herophile was the daughter of Zeus and Lamia and the first woman to chant oracles. They also preserved traditions about the Herophiles and other prophetically inspired figures.

l: Nymphs, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The second Herophile said that her mother was one of the Nymphs of Mount Ida and that she was connected with Mount Ida through her mother. Nymphs were also associated with her tomb, and other prophetic figures were said to have been inspired by Nymphs.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Delphi was one of the places visited by the second Herophile, who was said to have chanted while standing on the projecting stone there.

l: Mount Ida, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Mount Ida was identified as the region connected with the second Herophile through her mother, one of its Nymphs. The text also describes its thin, porous, red, and very dry soil as the reason the river Aidoneus disappears into the ground.

l: Marpessus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Marpessus was described as the second Herophile’s native place and as sacred to her mother. Its ruins remained on Trojan Ida, with about sixty inhabitants, and it was said to be 240 stades from Alexandria in the Troad.

l: Troad, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The second Herophile died in the Troad, where her tomb was located in the grove of Sminthian Apollo. Marpessus, associated with her origins, was also located in the Troad.

l: projecting stone, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The projecting stone above Delphi was said by the Delphians to be the place where the first Herophile chanted her oracles. The second Herophile was also said to have stood on this stone when she chanted.

l: oracles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The oracles attributed to the Herophiles included predictions about Helen, the ruin of Asia Minor and Europe, and the capture of Ilium by the Greeks. The text also mentions oracles delivered by Demo and other prophetically inspired figures.

l: divine inspiration, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Divine inspiration was the means by which Phaennis and the Peleae at Dodona prophesied, although they were not called Sibyls. Euclus, Musaeus, Lycus, and Bacis were also said to have been inspired by Nymphs.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Dropion, son of Deon and king of the Pæonians, sent a brazen head of a Pæonian bison to Delphi. The text describes how Pæonian bisons were captured by driving them onto slippery hides, weakening them with hunger, and then taming them with husked pinenuts. Delphi contained numerous offerings from the Phocians, Thessalians, Macedonians, Cyrenæans, Tarentines, and other Greeks, including groups depicting conflicts involving Apollo and Hercules. After the battle of Platæa, the Greeks dedicated a gold tripod on a bronze dragon, but Phocian leaders later took away the golden part.

l: Pæonian bison, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Pæonian bisons are described as exceptionally difficult to capture alive because ordinary nets cannot hold them. Hunters drive them into a palisaded hollow, make them slip down a slope covered with hides, weaken them through hunger, and finally tame them with husked pinenuts before binding and leading them away.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Delphi received the brazen head of a Pæonian bison and many other votive offerings from peoples including the Phocians, Thessalians, Macedonians, Cyrenæans, Tarentines, and Greeks generally. Its temple traditions also include the contests of Hercules and Apollo over a tripod.

l: brazen head of the Pæonian bison, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The brazen head was sent to Delphi by Dropion, the son of Deon and king of the Pæonians. It stood opposite a statue of Andreus, the founder of Andros.

l: Phocians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Phocians dedicated statues of Apollo, Athene, and Artemis at Delphi from spoil taken from the Thessalians. They also dedicated Hercules and other brazen figures connected with their fighting against the Thessalians in the Sacred War, and their leaders later abstracted the golden part of the tripod dedicated after the battle of Platæa.

l: Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Thessalians were described as constant enemies and neighbors of the Phocians, except where the Epicnemidian Locrians intervened. Thessalians of Pharsalus made votive offerings at Delphi, including Achilles on horseback with Patroclus running beside him, while their cavalry was defeated by the Phocians in the second encounter.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Apollo was represented among the Phocian offerings and in a group showing him about to fight Hercules for possession of a tripod, while Leto and Artemis tried to calm him. The Macedonians at Dium also dedicated an Apollo holding a doe, and a brazen Apollo from Mantinea stood near the treasury of the Corinthians.

l: Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Athene was included among the statues dedicated by the Phocians from spoil taken from the Thessalians. In the group depicting the contest between Hercules and Apollo, she tried to appease Hercules.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Artemis was included among the Phocian statues dedicated at Delphi from Thessalian spoil. In the group depicting the contest over the tripod, she joined Leto in trying to appease Apollo.

l: Sacred War, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Sacred War was the conflict in which the Thebans dedicated a statue of Hercules at Delphi while fighting the Phocians. The Phocians also dedicated a group depicting Hercules and Apollo in connection with their campaign against the Thessalians led by Tellias of Elis.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Hercules appeared in a group at Delphi fighting Apollo for possession of a tripod, with Athene attempting to calm him. When Hercules the son of Amphitryon consulted the oracle after killing Iphitus, Xenoclea initially refused to answer him; he seized and carried away the tripod, then returned it after she identified him as a different Hercules from the Egyptian Hercules.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: After the battle of Platæa, the Greeks jointly dedicated a gold tripod standing on a bronze dragon.

l: battle of Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: After the battle of Platæa, the Greeks made a common votive offering consisting of a gold tripod on a bronze dragon. The bronze part remained at Delphi, but the golden part had been taken away by Phocian leaders.

l: golden tripod, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The golden tripod was part of the joint Greek offering made after the battle of Platæa. Although the bronze dragon remained at Delphi, the golden part had been abstracted by the Phocian leaders.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The unit recounts the legend of Tennes, son of Cycnus, whose cutting of his father’s mooring ropes gave rise to the proverb of the Tenedian axe and whose island became known as Tenedos. It describes Greek dedications at Olympia and Delphi after the battles of Artemisium and Salamis, as well as Themistocles’ failed attempt to dedicate Persian spoils to Apollo. It also explains the Delphians’ bronze wolf, made after a wolf led them to sacred treasure stolen by a man and hidden on Mount Parnassus.

l: Tenedian axes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Tenedian axes are connected with the legend of Tennes, who cut the ropes of his father Cycnus’s ship with an axe when Cycnus came seeking his forgiveness. This act gave rise to a proverb for someone who obstinately refuses discussion and cuts a matter short.

l: Cycnus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Cycnus was said to be the son of Poseidon and king of Colonæ in the Troad. After his second wife falsely accused his son Tennes, Cycnus cast Tennes and his sister Hemithea into the sea in a chest, later learned the truth, and sailed after Tennes to seek forgiveness.

l: Leucophrys, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Leucophrys was the island where Tennes and Hemithea safely arrived after being sent to sea in a chest. It was later called Tenedos after Tennes.

l: Tennes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Tennes was the son of Cycnus and Proclea and the brother of Hemithea. After being falsely accused by Phylonome, he was cast into the sea with his sister, reached Leucophrys, cut the ropes of Cycnus’s ship when his father sought forgiveness, and was later said to have been killed by Achilles while defending Tenedos.

l: Tenedos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Tenedos was formerly called Leucophrys and received its later name from Tennes. Its people were eventually joined to the people of Alexandria on the mainland of the Troad because they were weak.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Greeks who fought against the King of the Persians dedicated a bronze Zeus at Olympia and an Apollo at Delphi after the actions at Artemisium and Salamis.

l: Persians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Persians were defeated in the actions at Artemisium and Salamis, and their spoils were brought as possible offerings to Apollo. The invasion by the Persians was said to have been foretold in the oracles of Bacis and in the earlier verses of Euclus.

l: Medes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Medes are associated with the Persian invasion and with the spoils that Themistocles brought to Delphi as a proposed offering to Apollo. One explanation for Apollo’s refusal was that Themistocles would later become a suppliant of the Persians, and acceptance might have brought him the undying hatred of the Medes.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Delphi received a Greek dedication of Apollo after Artemisium and Salamis. Themistocles went there to consult the Pythian Priestess and to offer spoils of the Medes, but the offering was rejected.

l: Themistocles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Themistocles brought spoils of the Medes to Delphi and asked whether he should offer them inside Apollo’s temple. The Pythian Priestess ordered him to remove them, and some interpreted the refusal as connected with his later status as a suppliant of the Persians.

l: spoils of the Medes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The spoils of the Medes were brought by Themistocles to Delphi as a proposed gift to Apollo. The Pythian Priestess ordered that they not be placed in the temple and that they be sent away as quickly as possible.

l: Pythian Priestess, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Pythian Priestess told Themistocles not to place the beautiful spoils of the Persians in Apollo’s temple. She instructed him to remove them and send them home as quickly as possible.

l: oracle of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The oracle of Apollo rejected Themistocles’ proposed dedication of Persian spoils. Its response ordered that the spoils not enter the temple and suggested that they be sent home immediately.

l: invasion of Greece by the barbarian, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The invasion of Greece by the barbarian was said to have been foretold in the oracles of Bacis and, earlier, in the verses of Euclus.

l: bronze wolf, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The bronze wolf stands near the great altar and was dedicated by the Delphians themselves. It commemorates a wolf that killed a man who had stolen the god’s treasures and then led the Delphians to the hidden sacred gold.

l: Delphians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Delphians followed a wolf that repeatedly ran into the town and howled, believing that its behavior was divinely directed. They discovered sacred gold hidden by a thief and dedicated a bronze wolf to the god.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: At Delphi, several statues and offerings commemorate victories involving Apollo, including victories over the Medes, Athenians, and Galati. Phaennis foretold the Galati's invasion of Asia and the rise of Attalus, whom she described through the image of a bull-horned helper. The Athenians dedicated a bronze palm and gilt statue of Athene for their victory at the Eurymedon, but gold was later removed from the statue. Clitodemus attributed this damage, along with other prodigies, to crows that appeared before the Athenians' expedition to Sicily.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Apollo has several statues at Delphi, including offerings from the Epidaurians, Megarians, people of Heraclea near the Euxine, the Amphictyones, and the Ætolians. The Delphians call one statue Sitalcas, and it is about 35 cubits high.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Athenians dedicated a bronze palm and a gilt statue of Athene at Delphi for their victory over land and river at the Eurymedon. Clitodemus says that crows later damaged the statue and related objects when the Athenians were preparing for their expedition to Sicily.

l: Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Galati are described as a Celtic army that would cross from Europe into Asia and destroy cities there. Phaennis foretold that they would ravage Asia and that Attalus would bring them a day of destruction.

l: Phaennis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Phaennis foretold, a generation in advance, that the army of the Celts would pass from Europe to Asia. She also foretold that a bull-horned helper, identified as Attalus, would destroy the Galati.

l: oracle about the Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The oracle says that the Galati would cross the Hellespont, devastate Asia, and afflict those living near the sea. It also says that Cronion would raise up a helper, identified as Attalus, who would bring destruction to the Galati.

l: Attalus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Attalus, king of Pergamus, is identified as the bull-horned helper in Phaennis's oracle. The bull image signifies that he would bring a day of destruction to the Galati.

l: bronze palm and gilt statue of Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Athenians dedicated the bronze palm and gilt statue of Athene at Delphi for their victory at the Eurymedon on land and river. Some of the gold was later missing; Clitodemus says crows tore it away and also broke the spear, owls, and fruit on the palm.

l: Sicily, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Sicily is the destination of the expedition for which the Athenians were making preparations when the crows appeared at Delphi. Clitodemus interpreted the crows' destruction of the statue and related objects as one of several prodigies intended to deter the Athenians from the expedition.

l: expedition to Sicily, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Athenians were preparing for the expedition to Sicily when, according to Clitodemus, an immense number of crows came to Delphi and damaged the statue of Athene and its accompanying objects. Clitodemus related this and other prodigies as warnings against the expedition.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Delphi contains numerous offerings and statues dedicated after military victories, including statues of Apollo, the bronze palm, and the gilt statue of Athene. It is also the place where crows were said to have damaged the Athenian dedication before the expedition to Sicily.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Lydian kings’ votive offerings to Apollo have disappeared except for the iron base of the bowl of Alyattes, made by Glaucus of Chios. Delphi contains offerings and statues from the Lacedæmonians, Ætolians, Elyrus, Carystians, and others, including representations connected with local victories and myths. In the seafight between the Liparæans and Tyrrhenians, the Liparæans captured several groups of ships after following the Pythian Priestess’s instructions and dedicated statues of Apollo at Delphi. Echecratides of Larissa dedicated a small Apollo, which the Delphians considered the first votive offering.

l: votive offerings, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Votive offerings at Delphi include the surviving iron base of the bowl of Alyattes, statues, a brazen goat, a brazen ox, and representations of generals and gods. They were dedicated by various peoples and individuals to commemorate myths, victories, prosperity, or successful warfare.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Apollo received the votive offerings described in this unit. The people of Elyrus said that Apollo fathered Phylacides and Philander with the Nymph Acacallis, and the Liparæans dedicated as many statues of Apollo as they had captured ships.

l: iron base of the bowl of Alyattes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The iron base of the bowl of Alyattes is the only remaining part of the votive offerings that the Lydian kings sent to Apollo. Glaucus of Chios made it by welding iron; its structure rises like a turret, has ladder-like iron girders, and supports the bowl at its outward-bending bars.

l: seafight between the Liparæans and Tyrrhenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: In the seafight between the Liparæans and Tyrrhenians, the Pythian Priestess instructed the Liparæans to fight with as small a fleet as possible. The Liparæans sailed with five triremes and captured the Tyrrhenians’ first five ships and three further groups of five.

l: Liparæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Liparæans followed the Pythian Priestess’s instruction to fight the Tyrrhenians with only five triremes. They captured four groups of five Tyrrhenian ships and dedicated at Delphi as many statues of Apollo as they had captured ships.

l: Tyrrhenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Tyrrhenians sailed against the Liparæans with five ships, thinking themselves a match for them. Their first fleet and three additional groups of five ships were captured by the Liparæans.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Delphi contains the white-stone object called the navel, which the Delphians considered the centre of the world. It also received numerous votive offerings, including the Liparæans’ statues of Apollo and Echecratides of Larissa’s small Apollo, which the Delphians regarded as the first votive offering.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The unit describes Sardinia, its geography, peoples, settlements, and successive colonizations. Libyans, Greeks, Iberes, Thespians, Athenians, and Trojans came to the island, while the Ilians, Corsi, and Balari later occupied its mountainous regions. The Carthaginians conquered most of Sardinia and built Caralis and Sulci, but the Ilians and Corsi resisted because of the protection offered by the mountains. The account also records Sardinia’s winds, climate, animals, plants, and the deadly grass associated with Sardonic laughter.

l: Sardinia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Sardinia is described as a large and prosperous island, called Ichnusa by the Greeks because of its footprint-like shape. It received successive settlers and colonists, including Libyans, Greeks, Iberes, Thespians, Athenians, and Trojans, and later contained settlements such as Nora, Olbia, Ogryle, Caralis, and Sulci. The island has mountainous regions, few harbours in the north, turbulent winds, pestilential air in some central areas, no serpents or wolves, unusually swift rams, and a deadly grass associated with Sardonic laughter.

l: Sardinians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Sardinians offered a brazen statue of Sardus, from whom the island was said to have taken its name. They called the Corsi by the name of their homeland and continued to honour Iolaus. Their island was eventually conquered by the Carthaginians except for the Ilians and Corsi.

l: Libyans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Libyans were said to have been the first people to cross into Sardinia under Sardus, though they joined rather than expelled the original inhabitants. They later crossed into the island again with a larger force, fought the Greeks, destroyed all but a remnant, and drove the Trojans into the mountains. Libyans or Iberes allied with the Carthaginians later quarrelled over the spoil and settled in the mountainous parts, where they were called Balari.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Greek traders called Sardinia Ichnusa, and later Greeks came to the island under Aristæus. Greeks and Trojans initially lived in Sardinia while the river Thorsus separated them from the barbarians, but the Greeks were eventually almost entirely destroyed by the returning Libyans. Thespians and Athenians under Iolaus built Olbia, while Athenians separately built Ogryle.

l: Trojans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: After the capture of Ilium, some Trojans who had escaped with Æneas were carried by the winds to Sardinia and mixed with the Greeks already there. After the Libyans defeated the Greeks, the Trojans fled to the island’s inaccessible mountains. Their descendants were called Ilians.

l: Ilians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Ilians were Trojans who occupied Sardinia’s rocky and difficult-to-access mountains after fleeing the Libyans. They were still called Ilians in the author’s time and resembled the Libyans in appearance, armour, and way of life. The Carthaginians did not reduce them to slavery because the mountains protected them.

l: Corsi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: The Corsi came from Cyrnus, which the Greeks called Corsica, after a large contingent crossed to Sardinia during factional conflict. They settled in part of Sardinia’s mountainous district and were named after their homeland. Like the Ilians, they avoided enslavement by the Carthaginians because of the security provided by the mountains.

l: Carthaginians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: When they became a great naval power, the Carthaginians subdued nearly all the Sardinians. They built the towns Caralis and Sulci and were allied with the Libyans or Iberes. Their conquest did not reduce the Ilians and Corsi to slavery because those peoples were protected by the mountains.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Achæans captured Phana after learning from a woman that its inhabitants depended on a single measured supply of water, which they fouled. At Delphi, the oracle had instructed them to observe how much water kept the inhabitants alive and how much the town had already drunk. The Ambraciotes dedicated a brazen ass after defeating the Molossi, whose planned night attack was disrupted by an ass pursuing a she-ass and braying. The account also mentions other votive offerings, including statues and representations dedicated after victories or fulfilled vows.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Achæans besieged Phana and, after consulting Delphi, captured it by fouling the town’s only water supply. They later offered a statue of Athene after reducing Phana.

l: Phana, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Phana was a fenced village in Ætolia whose inhabitants depended on a small, measured supply of water from a well near the walls. The Achæans captured it after making that water undrinkable.

l: siege of Phana, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The siege lasted a long time because the Achæans could not take Phana. They learned how to succeed after sending messengers to Delphi and discovering the town’s dependence on one well.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Achæans sent messengers to Delphi to ask how they could capture Phana. Delphi gave them an oracle directing their attention to the water that sustained the town.

l: oracle concerning the capture of Phana, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The oracle told the inhabitants of the land of Pelops and Achaia to observe how much water was daily given to Phana’s inhabitants and how much the town had already drunk. The Achæans initially failed to understand it, but later applied it by fouling the town’s water.

l: Ambraciotes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Ambraciotes detected the Molossi’s ambush after the disturbance caused by an ass and a she-ass. They attacked and defeated the Molossi that same night and offered a brazen ass.

l: brazen ass, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Ambraciotes offered a brazen ass after their night victory over the Molossi.

l: Molossi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Molossi prepared a night attack on the Ambraciotes. They were dismayed by the braying and disorderly noise of an ass and its driver, left their ambush, and were defeated.

l: night attack of the Molossi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The night attack was prepared by the Molossi against the Ambraciotes. An ass pursuing a she-ass disrupted the ambush, allowing the Ambraciotes to detect the plan and defeat them that night.

l: ass in the Molossian ambush, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The ass was being driven from the field when it pursued a she-ass with lust and brayed, while its driver shouted loudly and disorderly. The disturbance frightened the Molossi out of their ambush and contributed to their defeat.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: At Delphi, votive offerings commemorate Scyllis and his daughter Hydna, who helped wreck Xerxes’ fleet, while the temple’s gables and golden arms depict gods, heroes, and victories. The people of Methymna also sent Delphi a bronze image of Phallenian Dionysus after fishermen found a foreign-looking head at sea. The text recounts the Galati invasions of Greece, including their earlier expeditions under Cambaules and Bolgius and their large campaign under Brennus and Acichorius. Brennus persuaded the Galati to invade Greece for its wealth, assembling an army of 152,000 infantry and a cavalry force supported by servants under the custom called Trimarcisia.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Delphi contained votive offerings commemorating Scyllis and Hydna, including statues made by the Amphictyones, although Nero later took Hydna’s statue away. Its temple displayed representations of Artemis, Leto, Apollo, the Muses, the setting Sun, Dionysus, and the Thyiades, along with golden shields and Galatian arms. Delphi was the site of the greatest struggle between the Galati and the Greeks.

l: Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Galati made repeated expeditions toward Greece, first turning back from Thrace because they considered themselves too few, and later returning in greater strength. Their army was divided among commanders for campaigns against the Thracians, Triballi, Pæonians, Macedonians, and Illyrians. They later mustered 152,000 infantry and a cavalry force whose riders were supported by two mounted servants each.

l: irruption of the Galati into Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The irruption included an earlier expedition under Cambaules, a second expedition in which Bolgius fought the Macedonians and Illyrians, and a major invasion led by Brennus and Acichorius. The greatest struggle of this invasion against the Greeks took place at Delphi.

l: Celts, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Celts first crossed beyond their borders under Cambaules but did not advance beyond Thrace. In the second expedition, they defeated the Macedonians in battle after Ptolemy fell, though they did not proceed farther into Greece and returned home.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Greeks were the opponents of the Galati in the major invasion of Greece, whose greatest struggle occurred at Delphi. Brennus regarded Greece as weak at that period and sought to exploit its wealth and temple treasures.

l: Brennus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Brennus urged the assemblies and individual chieftains of the Galati to invade Greece, emphasizing its weakness and the wealth held in its communities and temples. He was chosen as a commander alongside Acichorius for the resulting campaign.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: Greece was targeted by the Galati because Brennus considered it weak and exceptionally wealthy in silver, gold, and temple offerings. The greatest confrontation between the Galati and the Greeks during the invasion took place at Delphi.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The Greeks, though dejected, resolve to fight the Galatians because they believe their survival and future security are at stake. The text compares the Greek forces at Thermopylæ during the Persian invasion with those assembled there against the Galatians, describing the latter contingents in detail. Greek forces destroy the bridges over the Sperchius to hinder the Galatian advance. Brennus responds by sending 10,000 troops across a marshy part of the river, forcing the Greek detachment there to withdraw to the main army.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The Greeks are said to have been very dejected but are induced by the urgency of the danger to fight bravely for their country. They assemble at Thermopylæ with contingents from several Greek regions, along with troops and ships from other allies, and send picked light-armed soldiers and cavalry to the Sperchius.

l: Celts, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The Galatians have crossed the ocean and are advancing through the region near Magnesia and Phthiotis. They cross the Sperchius by swimming through a marshy section and using their shields as rafts after the Greeks destroy the ordinary bridges.

l: Brennus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Brennus is described as intelligent and, for a barbarian, a capable strategist. He responds to the Greek defenses at the Sperchius by sending 10,000 troops to cross the river at a less-guarded marshy section.

l: Thermopylæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: Thermopylæ is the gathering place of the Greek forces opposing the Galatians. The text compares the much smaller Greek force that fought there during the Persian invasion with the larger allied force assembled there in the present conflict.

l: Sperchius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: The Greeks send about 1,000 picked light-armed soldiers and a troop of horse to the Sperchius to prevent the Galatians from crossing without a struggle. They destroy its bridges and camp nearby, but Galatian troops cross elsewhere, causing the Greek detachment to return to the main army.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: During the Persian invasion, Greek forces gathered at Thermopylæ under Leonidas and included contingents from Lacedæmon, Arcadia, Phocis, Locri, and other places. The text estimates the total force employed against the Persians at 11,200, although not all remained at Thermopylæ throughout the battle.

l: Galatian invasion of Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XX.
s: During the Galatian invasion, the Greeks believe that not only their liberty but also their future security is at stake. They assemble a substantial allied force at Thermopylæ, including infantry, cavalry, ships, and contingents from Bœotia, Phocis, Locri, Megara, Ætolia, Athens, Macedonia, and Asia.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Brennus led the Galati across the Sperchius toward Heraclea and Thermopylæ, seeking to force a route into Greece. At Thermopylæ, the Greeks defeated the Galati in a battle where the difficult terrain limited cavalry and the Athenians attacked from triremes. The Galati retreated in confusion, suffering heavy losses, and their dead were left unburied. The Athenians distinguished themselves, especially the young Cydias, who was killed in the fighting.

l: Brennus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Brennus ordered the inhabitants near the Maliac Bay to build bridges over the Sperchius, then led his army across them toward Heraclea. He advanced toward Thermopylæ after learning that a strong Greek force was gathered there, and he ordered an attack at daybreak despite having no Greek seer or, apparently, priests of his own country with him.

l: Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Galati ravaged the country around Heraclea and killed men found in the fields, but they did not capture the city because the Ætolians defended it. At Thermopylæ they fought with great fury despite inferior armour and difficult terrain, but were defeated and suffered heavy losses during their confused retreat. They did not ask permission to bury their dead and appeared indifferent to whether the bodies received burial.

l: Heraclea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Heraclea was protected by the Ætolians after its people had been compelled to join the Ætolian League the previous year. The Galati ravaged its surrounding country but did not capture the city.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Brennus sought to enter Greece by way of Thermopylæ after advancing from Heraclea.

l: Thermopylæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: Thermopylæ was the site where a strong force from the Greek cities confronted Brennus and the Galati. Its narrow, smooth, rocky ground and mountain streams made cavalry ineffective and contributed to the Galati's defeat and losses during their retreat.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Greeks assembled a strong force at Thermopylæ and advanced silently and in good order against the Galati. Their infantry maintained its line, while their light-armed troops used darts, arrows, and slings; after the battle they buried their dead and stripped the bodies of the barbarians.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: The Athenians sailed along the muddy arm of the sea in triremes and attacked the Galati's flanks with darts and arrows. They showed more valour than the other Greeks, especially the young Cydias, who fought for the first time and was killed by the Galati.

l: Battle of Thermopylæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXI.
s: In the Battle of Thermopylæ, the Greeks defeated the Galati, whose inferior armour and lack of experience were worsened by the narrow and rocky terrain. The Galati retreated in disorder, and many were trampled or lost in the marsh; 40 Greeks were killed, while the number of barbarian dead could not be accurately determined.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Seven days after the battle, Galati attempting to cross Mount Œta near Heraclea were defeated by a garrison commanded by Telesarchus, who was killed. Brennus sent Orestorius and Combutis with 40,000 infantry and about 800 cavalry into Ætolia, where they destroyed Callion and committed atrocities against its inhabitants. The Ætolians, joined by young men, old men, women, and some Achæans from Patræ, retaliated during the Galati retreat, and fewer than half of the 40,800 barbarians returned to Thermopylæ. Brennus then led 40,000 picked men through a pass over Mount Œta, defeated the Phocians guarding it, and forced the Greeks at Thermopylæ to disperse after the Athenians evacuated them by triremes.

l: Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Galati tried to cross Mount Œta near Heraclea and plunder a temple of Athene, but Telesarchus and his garrison defeated them. A force of 40,000 infantry and about 800 cavalry later devastated Callion and returned toward Thermopylæ, suffering heavy losses from the Ætolians and their allies. Brennus also led 40,000 picked Galati through a pass over Mount Œta, where they defeated the Phocians.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Greeks achieved successes against the barbarians at Mount Œta and defended Thermopylæ until Brennus reached their rear. After the Phocians were defeated and the Greeks risked being surrounded, the Athenians evacuated them by triremes, and the separate contingents dispersed.

l: Mount Œta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Mount Œta had a narrow pass near the ruins of Trachis and another, easier route through the district of the Ænianes. Galati were defeated while attempting one crossing, but Brennus later used the other pass to reach the rear of the Greek force at Thermopylæ.

l: Brennus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Brennus believed that forcing the Ætolians back into Ætolia would make war against the other Greeks easier. He sent Orestorius and Combutis into Ætolia, then arranged with the Ænianes and people of Heraclea to guide him through a pass over Mount Œta, while Acichorius attacked the Greek force from the front.

l: Ætolia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Ætolia was invaded by a selected Galati force under Orestorius and Combutis. After learning of Callion's destruction, the Ætolians returned there from Thermopylæ and fought to protect the remaining towns.

l: Callion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Callion was captured, plundered, and burned by the Galati. Its males, old men, and infants were butchered, while women and maidens suffered atrocities, suicide, or death from deprivation and abuse.

l: Ætolians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Ætolians left Thermopylæ rapidly after hearing of the disaster at Callion and gathered forces from their towns. Young men, old men, and women joined the army, and they attacked the retreating Galati with missiles along the roads. Their retaliation helped ensure that fewer than half of the 40,800 Galati returned safely to Thermopylæ.

l: Thermopylæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Thermopylæ was the main Greek defensive position when the Galati expedition returned from Ætolia. Brennus's passage over Mount Œta brought his forces to the Greek rear, after which the Athenians took the Greek troops aboard triremes and the contingents dispersed.

l: Phocians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Phocians guarded the pass over Mount Œta. A heavy mist prevented them from seeing Brennus's Galati until the attackers were close, and although the Phocians fought bravely, they were overpowered and withdrew to the main Greek force.

l: battle, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Seven days after the battle, a Galati force attempting to cross Mount Œta near Heraclea was defeated by the garrison under Telesarchus. Telesarchus fell during the action.

l: war against the other Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: Brennus thought that driving the Ætolians back into Ætolia would make the war against the other Greeks easier. His plan included sending a large Galati force into Ætolia and attacking the Greek position at Thermopylæ from the rear.

l: massacre at Callion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The massacre at Callion was carried out by the Galati after they captured the town. They killed males, old men, and infants, abused women, and committed acts of cannibalism and sexual violence; the Ætolians responded by pursuing and attacking the retreating Galati.

l: fight against the Galati at Thermopylæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXII.
s: The Greek defense at Thermopylæ was threatened when Brennus used a pass through the district of the Ænianes to reach the defenders' rear. The Phocians were defeated at the pass, and the Athenians then evacuated the Greek force by triremes before the Greeks were completely surrounded.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Brennus led the Galati toward Delphi, where the Greeks, aided especially by the Phocians and Ætolians, defeated them amid earthquakes, storms, lightning, falling rocks, and a panic that caused the barbarians to kill one another. Brennus was wounded, retreated with the surviving Galati, and later committed suicide by drinking neat wine. Acichorius’s division was delayed and harried by the Ætolians, and the retreating barbarians were attacked repeatedly until none reached home from the force that crossed into Greece. The disaster occurred in Phocis during Anaxicrates’ archonship, while the remaining Celts returned to Asia Minor the following year.

l: Brennus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Brennus waited for Acichorius’s troops and then marched toward Delphi with the Galati. He was wounded in the battle, was carried away in a fainting condition, and later committed suicide by drinking neat wine, either from fear of or shame before his comrades.

l: Acichorius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Acichorius’s division followed Brennus and was delayed by Ætolian attacks on its rearguard, baggage, and stragglers. It joined Brennus’s fleeing forces only the night before the final retreat, while a detachment remained at Heraclea to guard the camp’s treasure.

l: Apollo Spodius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The god told the frightened inhabitants of Delphi not to fear because he would protect his own. He showed hostility toward the barbarians through violent ground-shaking, thunder, lightning, falling rocks, and the panic that caused them to slaughter one another.

l: Celts, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Celts suffered severe losses in battle, from the winter conditions, from falling rocks, from panic, and from starvation. The text states that the Celts crossed back to Asia Minor in the following year, while a footnote explains that this refers to the Celtic forces remaining in Macedonia and Thrace rather than Brennus’s destroyed army.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Greeks gathered at Delphi to fight Brennus and the Galati. They resisted the barbarians throughout the battle and then attacked them during their retreat, with Athenians, Bœotians, Phocians, Ætolians, Thessalians, and Malienses contributing to the defeat.

l: Phocians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Phocians came from all their towns to defend Delphi and used their knowledge of the terrain to attack the Celtic rear from the slopes of Parnassus. They also guarded their flocks and herds, reported the barbarians’ nighttime panic, and lost nearly 6,000 in battle, with more than 10,000 additional deaths in the winter night and panic.

l: Ætolians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Ætolians initially sent only a few men, but Philomelus later brought 1,200, while the flower of their army attacked Acichorius’s division. They repeatedly harried the retreating barbarians with javelins and other missiles and attacked them all the way to the river Sperchius.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Delphi was threatened by Brennus and the Galati, and its inhabitants sought protection at the oracle. Greek forces assembled there to defend it, and the battle that followed ended in the barbarians’ defeat.

l: Phocis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Phocis was the scene of the battle and the barbarians’ disastrous retreat. Nearly 6,000 Galati were slain there in battle, more than 10,000 died during the wintry night and panic, and as many more died from starvation.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Celtic expedition to Greece ended in the utter ruin of the invading force that reached Delphi. The surviving Celtic forces were attacked during their withdrawal, and the remaining Celts crossed back to Asia Minor the following year.

l: invasion of Delphi by Brennus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: In the battle of Delphi, Brennus’s Galati fought the Greeks while earthquakes, thunder, lightning, and falling rocks disrupted them. The Greeks attacked from the front and rear, and the Galati retreated after Brennus was wounded.

l: Galatian invasion of Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The Galatian invasion of Greece culminated in the march on Delphi and the destruction of the invading force in Phocis. The Galati were defeated by the Greeks, repeatedly harried during their retreat, and prevented from returning home.

l: panic among the Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: The panic among the Galati began during the night after their retreat, when some thought they heard approaching horses and enemies. It spread through the host, and in the darkness the Galati mistook one another for Greeks and killed one another in large numbers.

l: Brennus’ suicide, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIII.
s: Brennus’ suicide followed his wounding and the destruction suffered by his army. Although his wounds were not mortal, he drank neat wine freely and killed himself, apparently from fear of his comrades or shame over the calamity he had caused.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: At Delphi, the Seven Wise Men dedicated the sayings “Know thyself” and “Not too much of anything” to Apollo and inscribed them in the vestibule of the temple at Delphi. The temple also contains a statue of Homer, an oracle concerning Homer, an altar of Poseidon, statues of the Fates, an altar associated with Neoptolemus the son of Achilles, the iron Chair of Pindar, and another gold statue of Apollo. Homer is connected by different traditions with Ios and Cyprus, while Ios preserves tombs said to belong to Homer and Clymene. Outside the temple are the grave of Neoptolemus and the fountain Cassotis, whose water is said to inspire prophetic powers.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Delphi contains the temple at Delphi, where the sayings of the Seven Wise Men were inscribed and several objects associated with Apollo, Homer, Poseidon, the Fates, and Neoptolemus the son of Achilles were kept. The people of Delphi offer annual funeral rites at the grave of Neoptolemus.

l: The Seven Wise Men, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The Seven Wise Men are identified as Thales of Miletus, Bias of Priene, Pittacus of Mitylene, Cleobulus of Lindus, Solon of Athens, Chilo of Sparta, and, according to Plato, Myson of Chenæ instead of Periander. They came to Delphi, offered Apollo the sayings “Know thyself” and “Not too much of anything,” and inscribed them in the vestibule of the temple at Delphi.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Apollo received the famous sayings offered by the Seven Wise Men at Delphi. The temple contains an altar dedicated to Apollo, statues of Apollo as Arbiter of the Fates, and another statue of Apollo made entirely of gold.

l: temple of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The temple at Delphi has a vestibule bearing the sayings “Know thyself” and “Not too much of anything.” It contains a brazen statue of Homer, an oracle concerning Homer, an altar of Poseidon, statues of two Fates, an altar where the priest of Apollo slew Neoptolemus the son of Achilles, the iron Chair of Pindar, and another gold statue of Apollo.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: A brazen statue of Homer stands on a pillar at the temple at Delphi, beside an oracle concerning his fatherland, death, and the riddle of young boys. Ios and Cyprus each claim Homer, and traditions identify Clymene or Themisto as his mother; the text gives no private account of his country or age.

l: oracle concerning Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The oracle concerning Homer says that he was born to both fortunate and unfortunate destinies, had no fatherland but a motherland, and that Ios would receive his remains. It warns him against the riddle of young boys, which is explained as a tradition that Homer died of grief after failing to solve a riddle posed by fisher boys.

l: Ios, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Ios is identified by the oracle concerning Homer as the island that would receive Homer’s remains. Its inhabitants show Homer’s tomb and, elsewhere on the island, the tomb of Clymene, whom they say was Homer’s mother.

l: Cyprus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Cyprus is another place that claims Homer as its own. Its people say that Themisto was Homer’s mother and cite prophetic verses of Euclus that describe Homer’s birth in Cyprus, his departure by sea, and his singing of the woes of Hellas.

l: Neoptolemus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Neoptolemus the son of Achilles was slain by the priest of Apollo at an altar in the temple at Delphi. His grave lies in precincts outside the temple, and the people of Delphi offer him funeral rites annually.

l: grave of Neoptolemus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: The grave of Neoptolemus lies in precincts to the left of the temple at Delphi. The people of Delphi perform annual funeral rites there.

l: Cassotis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIV.
s: Cassotis is a walled fountain reached by an ascent through the wall near the temple at Delphi. Its water is said to run underground and inspire the women in the sanctuary of Apollo with prophetic powers, and its name is attributed to one of the Nymphs of Parnassus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Lounge is a building at Delphi containing Polygnotus’s paintings, including a scene of the capture of Ilium and the Greeks’ preparations to sail home. The painting shows Menelaus preparing to depart, while Phrontis, his pilot, is remembered as having died near Sunium and Menelaus as having stayed behind for his funeral rites. It also depicts Helen, Æthra, Andromache, Polyxena, Nestor, and many other figures associated with the fall of Ilium and its aftermath. The Trojan women appear dejected, as though they are already captives.

l: The Lounge, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Lounge is a building above the fountain at Delphi containing paintings by Polygnotus. It is a votive offering of the people of Cnidos, and the people of Delphi call it The Lounge because they formerly assembled there to discuss serious and trifling subjects.

l: Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Polygnotus painted scenes of the capture of Ilium and the Greeks’ return in The Lounge. He depicted Phrontis accurately according to Homer and represented several wounded warriors in accordance with Lescheos’s poem, suggesting that he had read it; the narrator thinks he invented the other names in the group.

l: the capture of Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The capture of Ilium is represented in a painting in The Lounge, together with the Greeks’ preparations for their departure. The scene includes the Trojan women as dejected captives and shows events involving Helen, Æthra, Andromache, Polyxena, and others.

l: Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Ilium is shown in connection with its capture and the return of the Greeks. Lescheos says that Æthra escaped from Ilium when it was taken and reached the Greek camp.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Greeks are depicted preparing to sail after the capture of Ilium. Their ships and tents are shown, and Menelaus is preparing to hoist sail while some of the Greeks take down his tent.

l: Menelaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Menelaus is shown preparing to hoist sail after the capture of Ilium. He had been sailing with Nestor but stayed behind near Sunium to perform the proper funeral rites for Phrontis, his pilot.

l: Phrontis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Phrontis, the son of Onetor, is depicted as the pilot of Menelaus’s ship, standing in its middle with two punting poles. Homer describes him as highly skilled, and says that he died while sailing past Sunium in Attica; Menelaus stayed behind to perform his funeral rites.

l: Nestor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Nestor is depicted in the painting wearing a hat and carrying a spear, with a horse near him rolling in the dust. Homer is cited as describing Nestor telling Telemachus about Phrontis, and Nestor had been sailing with Menelaus before Menelaus stayed behind at Phrontis’s death.

l: Helen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Helen is depicted seated, with Eurybates near her and her handmaids Panthalis and Electra beside her. Eurybates is thought to be delivering Agamemnon’s message asking Helen to consent to Demophon’s request for Æthra, and Helen gives her consent.

l: Æthra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Æthra, the mother of Theseus, is depicted next to Helen with her head shaven. Lescheos says that she escaped when Ilium was taken, reached the Greek camp, and was recognized by the sons of Theseus; Demophon asked Agamemnon for her, and Helen consented to release her.

l: Andromache, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Andromache is depicted among the Trojan women with a baby boy at her breast. Lescheos says that the baby was later hurled from a tower because of Neoptolemus’s private hatred, rather than by decree of the Greeks.

l: Polyxena, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: Polyxena is depicted with her hair plaited in the manner of maidens. The poets say that she was slain at the tomb of Achilles, and the narrator has seen paintings of her death at Athens and Pergamus beyond the river Caicus.

l: the Trojan women, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The Trojan women in the painting look sorrowful and dejected, as if they are already captives. They include Andromache, Medesicaste, and Polyxena.

l: the painting of Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXV.
s: The painting of Polygnotus depicts the capture of Ilium and the Greeks’ return, including Menelaus’s ship, tents being taken down, Helen, Trojan women, wounded warriors, Nestor, and a horse rolling near the seashore. It includes a shoreline with visible pebbles, although the rest of the scene does not resemble a sea view.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Polygnotus’s painting depicts the fall of Troy, including the captives Clymene, Creusa, Aristomache, Xenodice, Deinome, Metioche, Pisis, Cleodice, and Laodice. It shows Epeus knocking down Troy’s walls, the Wooden Horse, several Greek heroes, and Ajax the son of Oileus swearing an oath concerning the violation of Cassandra. Neoptolemus is shown killing Trojan men, while Cassandra clings to the wooden statue of Athene at the altar. The painting also includes Medusa, an old shaven-headed figure or eunuch, and a frightened child.

l: Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Polygnotus painted scenes of Troy’s destruction, including Epeus knocking down the walls, the Wooden Horse, Ajax’s oath concerning the violation of Cassandra, and Neoptolemus killing Trojan men. He is said to have invented the names Metioche, Pisis, and Cleodice, since they are not mentioned by the cited poets.

l: Troy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Troy is depicted as being attacked and destroyed: Epeus knocks down its walls, and the Wooden Horse appears above them. The painting also shows the slaughter of Trojan men.

l: Wooden Horse, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Wooden Horse is represented by its head alone above the walls of Troy. It is painted near the figures associated with the fall of the city.

l: Odysseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Odysseus is depicted wearing a coat of mail. He and Menelaus are said to have been entertained by Antenor, and Odysseus recognized and rescued Helicaon during the night-engagement.

l: Ajax the son of Oileus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Ajax the son of Oileus stands near the altar with a shield in his hand and takes an oath concerning the violation of Cassandra. The sons of Atreus administer the oath to him.

l: Cassandra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Cassandra is shown seated on the ground and holding fast to the wooden statue of Athene. She had torn the statue from its base when Ajax dragged her away from the altar.

l: Menelaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Menelaus is depicted wearing a helmet, and his shield bears the image of the dragon that appeared to him as an omen during the sacrifice at Aulis. He and Odysseus were entertained by Antenor, and their affection for Antenor’s family is given as a reason that Laodice was probably spared.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Greeks are represented through figures including Epeus, Polypoetes, Acamas, Odysseus, Ajax, Menelaus, and Neoptolemus. They administer an oath to Ajax concerning the violation of Cassandra, and they are said to have spared Laodice because of their regard for Antenor’s family.

l: Trojans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The Trojans are shown suffering during the sack of Troy. Neoptolemus is represented as continuing to butcher the Trojans, killing Elasus and Astynous among them.

l: Neoptolemus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Neoptolemus is depicted killing Elasus, whose dying agony is said to be well represented, and striking the kneeling Astynous with a sword. Polygnotus portrayed him as the only Greek who continued to butcher the Trojans, corresponding to scenes on Neoptolemus’s tomb.

l: altar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The altar appears in the scene involving Ajax and Cassandra, with Ajax standing near it and Cassandra holding the statue of Athene. Another altar is shown with a frightened little boy clinging to it and a brazen coat of mail lying upon it.

l: Laodice, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: Laodice is painted standing on the other side of the altar. Although she is not named by the cited poets among the captive Trojan women, it is considered probable that the Greeks let her go because Menelaus and Odysseus were favorably disposed toward her husband’s family.

l: captives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The captives depicted between Æthra and Nestor include Clymene, Creusa, Aristomache, and Xenodice. Deinome, Metioche, Pisis, and Cleodice are shown reclining above them, while Laodice is painted near the altar.

l: violation of Cassandra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVI.
s: The violation of Cassandra is the subject of an oath taken by Ajax the son of Oileus. Ajax stands near the altar with a shield while the sons of Atreus administer the oath.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The painting depicts numerous Trojan dead, including Pelis, Eioneus, Admetus, Leocritus, Coroebus, Priam, Axion, Agenor, Echeclus, Sinon, Anchialus, Eresus, and Laomedon. It presents differing accounts by Lescheos and other poets concerning who killed several figures and what happened to Hecuba and Priam. The painting also shows Antenor’s household being spared by the Greeks, with Theano, their children, servants, and baggage depicted sorrowfully. Simonides’ elegiac couplet identifies Polygnotus of Thasos as the painter of these incidents in the capture of Ilium.

l: Neoptolemus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Neoptolemus is said to have killed Eioneus, Coroebus, Priam, and Agenor. Lescheos states that Neoptolemus tore Priam away from the altar and killed him at the palace doors.

l: Lescheos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Lescheos gives accounts of the deaths of Eioneus, Admetus, Coroebus, Priam, Axion, and Agenor. He says that Priam was killed at the palace doors rather than at the altar of Household Zeus, and that Coroebus was killed by Diomede.

l: Odysseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Odysseus is said to have killed Leocritus, the son of Polydamas. His companion Sinon is depicted carrying Laomedon’s corpse for burial.

l: Coroebus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Coroebus, the son of Mygdon, came to wed Cassandra and was killed by Neoptolemus according to the prevalent tradition, but by Diomede according to Lescheos. He is depicted among the dead above Eioneus and Admetus.

l: Priam, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Priam is depicted among the dead above Coroebus. Lescheos says that Neoptolemus tore him away from the altar of Household Zeus and killed him without great difficulty at the palace doors.

l: Antenor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
