s: Antenor’s house is depicted with a leopard’s skin over the porch as a sign to the Greeks not to harm his family. Antenor is shown standing near his daughter Crino, while his wife Theano and sons Glaucus and Eurymachus are also depicted.

l: Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Polygnotus of Thasos, the son of Aglaophon, is identified by Simonides as the painter of the depicted incidents in the capture of Ilium.

l: Lescheos’s account of the Trojan dead, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Lescheos’s account identifies Eioneus as slain by Neoptolemus, Admetus by Philoctetes, Coroebus by Diomede, Axion by Eurypylus, and Agenor by Neoptolemus. It also states that Priam was killed at the palace doors after being torn away from the altar.

l: the capture of Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The capture of Ilium is represented through scenes of Trojan deaths, the carrying out of Laomedon’s corpse, and the guarded household of Antenor. Simonides’ inscription says that Polygnotus painted these incidents.

l: Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: Ilium is the city whose capture is depicted in the painting. The scenes include its dead, Laomedon’s burial, and the preservation of Antenor’s household.

l: the painting of Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The painting shows Trojan dead, including Priam and Coroebus, as well as Sinon and Anchialus carrying Laomedon’s corpse. It also depicts Antenor’s household, servants loading belongings onto an ass, and a child sitting on the animal; Simonides’ couplet identifies Polygnotus of Thasos as its painter.

l: incidents in the capture of Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVII.
s: The incidents include the deaths of Trojan figures, the removal of Laomedon’s corpse for burial, and the depiction of Antenor’s family under a sign warning the Greeks not to harm them. Simonides attributes their painting to Polygnotus of Thasos.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The left part of Polygnotus’ painting depicts Odysseus descending to Hades to consult Tiresias about returning home. It shows Acheron, Charon’s boat, Tellis, Cleobœa, a son being strangled by his father, a sacrilegious wretch receiving punishment, Eurynomus, Auge, and Iphimedea. The passage also discusses the Minyad’s account of Theseus and Pirithous, reverence for fathers, and piety to the gods. Eurynomus is described as a demon who eats the flesh of the dead, although he is not mentioned in the Odyssey, the Minyad, or The Return from Ilium.

l: the painting, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The painting depicts scenes in Hades, including Odysseus’ descent, Charon’s boat on Acheron, the punishment of people who mistreated fathers or committed sacrilege, and several named figures. It also includes Eurynomus, Auge, and Iphimedea.

l: picture (Polygnotus’ painting), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The left part of the painting represents Odysseus descending to Hades to consult Tiresias about his return home. It contains Acheron, Charon and his boat, Tellis, Cleobœa, and various figures suffering or receiving honor in Hades.

l: Odysseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Odysseus is represented as descending to Hades to consult Tiresias about his return home.

l: Hades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Hades is the setting for the painting’s scenes of the dead and their punishments. Eurynomus is described as a demon in Hades who eats the flesh of the dead.

l: Tiresias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Tiresias is the soul whom Odysseus visits in Hades to consult about his return home.

l: Acheron, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Acheron is represented as a river in the painting, with reeds, indistinct fish, and Charon’s boat.

l: Charon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Charon is represented as an old ferryman rowing a boat on Acheron. The Minyad says that he unwillingly admitted the living Theseus and Pirithous into his boat meant for the dead.

l: the Minyad, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The Minyad contains an account of Theseus and Pirithous entering Charon’s boat while still alive. It is also named as one of the poems containing accounts of Hades and its horrors.

l: Tellis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Tellis appears in Charon’s boat looking like a youth. The text says that Archilochus was his great-grandson.

l: Cleobœa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Cleobœa appears in Charon’s boat as a virgin, holding a cist used in the worship of Demeter. She is said to have first introduced the mysteries of Demeter from Paros to Thasos.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Demeter is associated with the cist that Cleobœa holds in the painting and with the mysteries that Cleobœa is said to have introduced from Paros to Thasos.

l: sacrilegious wretch, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The sacrilegious wretch is depicted near the man who mistreated his father, suffering punishment in Hades.

l: punishment of the sacrilegious wretch, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: The punishment of the sacrilegious wretch is represented in Polygnotus’ painting. A woman who appears familiar with poison and other harmful things is shown punishing him.

l: piety to the gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Piety to the gods is illustrated by the Athenians’ treatment of the temple of Olympian Zeus at Syracuse and by Datis’ conduct toward the Delians and a statue of Apollo. Polygnotus included the sacrilegious wretch’s punishment because people in earlier times honored the deity.

l: Eurynomus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Eurynomus is described by the Antiquarians at Delphi as a demon in Hades who eats the flesh of the dead down to their bones. In the painting he is blueish-black, shows his fangs, and sits on a vulture’s skin; he is not mentioned in the Odyssey, the Minyad, or The Return from Ilium.

l: Auge, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Auge appears in the painting near Eurynomus. She came to Teuthras in Mysia and bore a son by Hercules who was said to resemble him more than the sons born to Hercules by any other woman.

l: Iphimedea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Iphimedea appears in the painting near Eurynomus. The Carians living at Mylasa treat her with very great honor.

l: Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXVIII.
s: Polygnotus painted the left part of the painting with Odysseus’ descent to Hades, Acheron, Charon, and several figures receiving punishment or honor. He followed the Minyad’s description of Theseus and Pirithous entering Charon’s boat and included Eurynomus despite that figure not appearing in the cited poems.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: The unit describes figures in Polygnotus’ picture, including Ocnus making rope while a she-ass eats it, Ariadne watching Phædra, and several women associated with myths of the underworld. Dionysus is said to have taken Ariadne from Theseus and to have invaded India and built a bridge over the Euphrates. Odysseus summons the dead while Tiresias approaches, and Theseus and Pirithous sit on an enchanted rock after their attempt to rescue Persephone. The text also discusses the friendship of Theseus and Pirithous, citing Homer and Panyasis.

l: Odysseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Odysseus is shown kneeling beside a ditch with his sword held over it, while Tiresias approaches and his mother Anticlea sits nearby. He is also associated with Perimedes and Eurylochus and with the Homeric account of seeing former heroes such as Theseus and Pirithous.

l: Ocnus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Ocnus is represented seated and making rope while a she-ass eats the rope as quickly as he makes it. He is said to have been industrious but married to an extravagant wife who quickly spent whatever he gathered, and his name is used for a person laboring hard to no profit.

l: Polygnotus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXIX.
s: Polygnotus represents Ocnus making rope with a she-ass consuming it, apparently as a skit on Ocnus’ wife. His picture also includes Ariadne, Phædra, and the other figures described in this unit.
